Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Vignette:
Dmitri Voss is a 50-year-old European American clinical psychologist who presented for intake following a sexual assault that occurred approximately eight months prior. He is married, maintains a private practice, and had, until recently, built a professional identity around his capacity to sit with others in their most acute distress. That identity is now something he can barely recognize.

The assault took place late on a Friday evening after Dmitri attended a professional development dinner. A colleague he had known for several years offered to walk him to his car in the parking structure. The details of what followed remain fractured and inaccessible in ways that Dmitri finds deeply disorienting, particularly given his clinical training. What he does retain is sensory: the smell of alcohol on the man's breath, close and overwhelming; the distant wail of a siren somewhere on the street below the structure that no one responded to; the concrete surface of the wall against his back. He recalls a point at which he stopped forming coherent thoughts and simply endured. He drove himself home that night. He did not tell his wife.

In the weeks that followed, Dmitri noticed that something had changed in how he moved through his own memories. When fragments of that evening began to surface, he found himself pushing them back before they could fully take shape — not as a deliberate strategy but as something that simply happened, a door swinging shut before he could see what was behind it. More unsettling still, there were moments when he could not locate any image at all, no scene, no face, no sequence of events, yet the full weight of what he had felt that night would descend on him without warning — a crushing, formless dread that arrived in the middle of an ordinary afternoon. He had no clinical language that felt adequate to describe this to himself. He could not seem to put the experience into words, and for a man whose entire professional life was built on the precise articulation of psychological experience, this was its own particular wound.

His triggers arrived without mercy in the texture of daily life. The smell of alcohol — at a restaurant, in the hand sanitizer a patient used before a session, in a glass of wine his wife poured at dinner — would arrest him completely. The sound of sirens passing his office building on a busy street in the city could stop him mid-sentence with a client. Even the vaguer sensation of simply feeling uncomfortable in a room, a slight physical unease, had become a signal his body treated as catastrophic.

Over months, Dmitri began quietly restructuring his practice. He stopped taking new trauma referrals, telling himself it was a caseload issue. He rescheduled or cancelled sessions on days when he felt least able to hold the room. His wife noticed he had become remote, that he seemed to be going through the motions of their life together, and she had said so more than once. He had not explained. What frightened him most was not that she would be angry but that she would look at him with pity, or worse, with the particular clinical softness he himself had offered to patients — and that he would feel, as he increasingly did, like something acted upon rather than a person capable of acting.

He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that the man he had been before — the clinician, the husband, the person who understood suffering and helped others metabolize it — was simply gone. He described feeling dead inside during the intake, not metaphorically but as a flat statement of fact. He felt like an object, he said, not a person. He no longer felt capable of the work that had defined him for twenty years.

What finally brought Dmitri to seek help was a session in which a patient disclosed a sexual assault and he realized, with horror, that he had nothing to offer. He sat across from her and felt entirely hollow. He scheduled his own intake the following morning. What he hopes for, he said quietly, is to find out whether there is anything left of himself to recover. What he is most afraid of is that the answer is no.
